newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Seventy Indonesians questioned over ethnic riots.
newsitem.headline: Seventy Indonesians questioned over ethnic riots.

text.p: Indonesian police have questioned 70 people accused of involvement in recent ethnic rioting and will submit the dossiers of 11 to prosecutors, the official Antara news agency reported on Thursday.

The agency quoted Colonel Erwin Achmad, police chief of West Kalimantan province, as saying on Wednesday that the suspects had been accused of inciting the riots in the province by spreading rumours. They were also accused of assault, damage to property and illegal possession of sharp weapons.

He said police would soon submit the dossiers of 11 people to the prosecutor's office, adding that there was a possibility the number of suspects would increase because the investigation was still continuing.

"I don't know yet if the number of suspects will increase, but our investigation is still on," he was quoted as saying in Pontianak, the capital of West Kalimantan province. Antara gave no further details.

A clash began in West Kalimantan, on the Indonesian side of Borneo island, late in December between members of the native Dayak tribe and migrants from Madura island, which lies off the main Indonesian island of Java.

The clash in Sanggau Ledo, about 95 km (60 miles) north of Pontianak, was apparently sparked by a fight over a girl. Further violence rooted in long-standing ethnic rivalry resumed in late January and continued as recently as last week. About 3,000 troops have been deployed to contain the unrest.

Indonesian armed forces commander General Feisal Tanjung was quoted by the Jakarta Post last week as saying the conflict had been ended by a peace pact signed by the warring parties. Most Dayaks are Christians while the Maduran migrants are Moslems.
Tanjung also denied reports that about 300 people had been killed in the riots and said he would soon announce the official death toll.
Military officials and residents of the province had previously said at least 12 people had been killed over the past six weeks.
